tagline: An early freeway follows the Arroyo Seco through tunnels and tight interchanges
intro: The Arroyo Seco Parkway connects Los Angeles and Pasadena beside a seasonal river, with northbound tunnels through Elysian Park and tight entrance and exit curves. An archived Federal Highway Administration profile describes this National Scenic Byway as a blend of landscaped parkway and modern freeway, passing through the Arroyo Seco’s historic Arts and Crafts landscape.

Early plans competed over the road’s purpose: recreation in a park setting or a fast connection between the cities. By the mid-1930s, commuter needs had overtaken the recreational emphasis. Construction began in 1938, and most of the parkway opened in 1940. Engineers designed for 45 miles per hour, retaining parkway features such as roadside native plantings. Local streets sometimes served as ramps, ending in sharp right turns where a conventional interchange would not fit.

Northbound, begin at the Four Level Interchange, pass through the Figueroa Street Tunnels and cross the Los Angeles River. The original road then follows the Arroyo Seco’s west bank, passing beneath the Santa Fe railroad bridge before crossing the stream into South Pasadena. Beyond Fair Oaks Avenue it turns north past Raymond Hill and reaches Pasadena. The freeway ends at Glenarm Street; Arroyo Parkway continues as a city street toward Colorado Boulevard.

moments.title: Figueroa Street Tunnels
moments.text: Four tunnels carry northbound State Route 110 through Elysian Park. They began as a two-way road, with two lanes in each direction and a sidewalk along one side. The three northern tunnels opened in 1931 to provide a bypass of part of North Broadway. Once the parkway reached them, its six lanes narrowed to four at the tunnels and viaduct. A separate southbound road opened in 1943, leaving the older tunnels for northbound travel. The newer southbound lanes run higher through open cuts and cross the valleys between ridges on viaducts.

moments.title: Santa Fe Arroyo Seco Railroad Bridge
moments.text: Above the parkway in Highland Park, the Santa Fe Arroyo Seco Railroad Bridge carries Metro’s A Line. The span extends more than 710 feet and crosses the road at an elevation of over 56 feet. It replaced an 1889 wooden trestle, itself a replacement for an 1885 crossing. Mainline rail service ended in 1994. The bridge was then retrofitted for the Gold Line, which opened in 2003; the A Line took over these tracks after the Regional Connector opened in June 2023. The older wooden crossings carried the Southern California Railway and, before it, the Los Angeles and San Gabriel Valley Railroad.

moments.title: Pasadena
moments.text: At Glenarm Street, freeway driving gives way to Arroyo Parkway, a surface street continuing toward Colorado Boulevard. Colorado Boulevard and Arroyo Parkway once carried U.S. Route 66 through Pasadena. An earlier transport connection had helped reshape the city: Santa Fe service began stopping downtown in 1887, triggering a real-estate boom. Pasadena developed as a winter resort for wealthy Easterners, with new neighborhoods, business districts and links to Los Angeles. Rail travel preceded the parkway link, which connected the city to downtown Los Angeles in 1940. Old Pasadena is the city’s original commercial district.
